questions.q: What is the difference between an SLI, an SLO, and an SLA?
options: An SLI is the actual measured number, an SLO is the internal target, and an SLA is the external promise made to a consumer
They are three different names for the exact same concept
SLA is internal, SLO is external, and SLI doesn't apply to data pipelines
Only SLAs are ever used in real data engineering practice
questions.explain: All three measure the same underlying thing but serve different audiences and purposes.

questions.q: Why should an internal SLO be set stricter than the external SLA it supports?
options: SLOs and SLAs should always be set to the exact same number
A stricter SLO has no practical benefit over matching the SLA exactly
The SLA should always be stricter than the SLO, not the other way around
It builds in a buffer so normal operational noise and variance don't push the team past the actual consumer-facing promise
questions.explain: Setting the SLO equal to the SLA leaves no room for anything to go even slightly wrong before breaking a real promise.

options: The financial cost of missing an SLA
A count of how many alerts fired in a given month
The allowed slack in an SLO, turned into a spendable resource for risky changes like deploys or experiments
A fixed dollar amount allocated for Fabric Capacity billing
questions.explain: If the budget is used up, that's a concrete signal to slow down on risky changes and focus on stability instead.

questions.q: How does Lesson 52's observability work connect to SLIs specifically?
options: SLIs replace the need for any metrics or logs
Lesson 52's metrics are literally how an SLI gets measured
Observability and SLIs are unrelated concepts
Only traces, never metrics, can produce a valid SLI
questions.explain: This lesson isn't introducing new infrastructure — it's a disciplined way of using what was already built.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how should Lesson 53's alerts ideally be triggered in relation to SLOs?
options: Only when the SLA itself has already been broken
Alerts should never be tied to SLOs in any way
Every single time any metric deviates from the SLO target, no matter how small
Based on a trend that threatens to burn through the error budget, not on every single missed target
questions.explain: This avoids the alert fatigue problem from Lesson 53 while still giving a concrete, numeric answer to whether stability needs attention.
